title: Trump Sparks Fierce Backlash After Escalating Personal Attacks on Michigan Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed
snippet: President Donald Trump's intensified rhetoric targeting Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan's pivotal Senate race drew sharp condemnation from former allies and political opponents alike.
content:
PORT HURON, Mich. — With control of the U.S. Senate hanging in the balance, President Donald Trump escalated his political rhetoric over the weekend, launching a series of incendiary attacks against Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed that drew swift condemnation from former key allies.

Speaking at a rally in the border city of Port Huron on Sunday, Trump repeatedly attacked El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official aiming to become the nation's first Muslim senator. Trump branded El-Sayed a 'jihadist' aligned with terrorists and invoked the September 11 terrorist attacks, drawing comparisons between preventing El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the heroic efforts of passengers aboard Flight 93.

Rebukes from Former Allies

The president's sharp rhetoric triggered an immediate backlash, including from Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump—a group instrumental in driving Republican outreach to Michigan's Arab American voters in 2024. Bahbah publicly broke with Trump over the remarks, calling them 'racist' and 'out of line.'

'The president of the United States saying that about a person because of his religion, that is just not acceptable,' Bahbah said, warning that voters would remember the rhetoric when heading to the polls on Election Day.

High Stakes in Michigan

The battle between El-Sayed and Republican challenger Mike Rogers to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is among a handful of razor-thin contests that could determine control of the Senate. As Republicans face headwinds over inflation, energy costs, and foreign conflicts, the GOP campaign strategy has increasingly focused on questioning El-Sayed's national security credentials and alleging ties to the Muslim Brotherhood—claims for which there is no evidence.

El-Sayed pushed back forcefully during a campaign rally in Grand Rapids later Sunday alongside Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders. Addressing Trump's repeated attempts to mock his name, El-Sayed dismissed the attacks to cheering supporters. 'I don’t even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me ‘senator’ after November,' El-Sayed said. 'I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro.'

Sanders accused Trump and his allies of leaning into Islamophobia to distract from core economic issues, asserting that the GOP has 'nothing to say' regarding healthcare, housing, and income inequality.
